blocks.body:
Every real number can be approximated by fractions, since the rationals are dense. The interesting question is how well, measured against the size of the denominator. With denominator $q$ you can always get within $\frac1{2q}$ of $\alpha$, just by rounding $q\alpha$. Some numbers allow much better: $\frac{355}{113}$ is within $2.7\times10^{-7}$ of $\pi$, far closer than $\frac1{2\cdot113}$.

Diophantine approximation measures this by a power of $q$. It is a theory with two faces. A number that has extremely good rational approximations cannot be algebraic (Liouville, Roth). A number that has a sequence of good, but not perfect, approximations cannot be rational, which is how irrationality proofs such as Apéry's for $\zeta(3)$ work. And bounds on how well algebraic numbers can be approximated give finiteness theorems for Diophantine equations.

blocks.title: Irrationality exponent
blocks.body:
For real $\alpha$ the irrationality exponent $\mu(\alpha)$ is the supremum of all $\mu$ such that
$$0<\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|<\frac{1}{q^{\mu}}$$
has infinitely many solutions in rationals $\frac pq$ with $q\ge1$.

It measures how fast the best approximations converge: rationals have $\mu=1$, every irrational has $\mu\ge2$ (Dirichlet, below), algebraic irrationals have $\mu=2$ exactly (Roth), and numbers with $\mu=\infty$ are called Liouville numbers.

blocks.title: Dirichlet's approximation theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be real and $N\ge1$ an integer. There are integers $p,q$ with $1\le q\le N$ and $|q\alpha-p|<\frac1N$. If $\alpha$ is irrational, there are infinitely many rationals $\frac pq$ with
$$\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|<\frac{1}{q^2}.$$

Write $\{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$. The $N+1$ numbers $\{0\cdot\alpha\},\{1\cdot\alpha\},\dots,\{N\alpha\}$ lie in $[0,1)$, which is the union of the $N$ intervals $[\frac kN,\frac{k+1}N)$, $0\le k<N$. By the [[pigeonhole|pigeonhole principle]] two of them, say $\{i\alpha\}$ and $\{j\alpha\}$ with $0\le i<j\le N$, lie in the same interval, so $|\{j\alpha\}-\{i\alpha\}|<\frac1N$. With $q=j-i\in[1,N]$ and $p=\lfloor j\alpha\rfloor-\lfloor i\alpha\rfloor$ this says $|q\alpha-p|<\frac1N$. Dividing by $q$ and using $q\le N$: $|\alpha-\frac pq|<\frac1{qN}\le\frac1{q^2}$.

Now let $\alpha$ be irrational, so $|q\alpha-p|>0$ for every pair. Starting from one pair, choose $N$ larger than $1/|q\alpha-p|$; the new pair has a strictly smaller value of $|q\alpha-p|$. Repeating gives infinitely many pairs with values decreasing to $0$, each satisfying $|\alpha-\frac pq|<\frac1{q^2}$. They give infinitely many different fractions: the pairs representing one fraction $\frac{p_0}{q_0}$ in lowest terms are $(kp_0,kq_0)$ with $k\ge1$, and these have $|kq_0\alpha-kp_0|\ge|q_0\alpha-p_0|>0$, so only finitely many of our pairs can represent it.

blocks.title: Continued fractions find the best approximations
blocks.body:
Dirichlet's proof is not constructive, but [[continued-fractions|continued fractions]] produce the approximations explicitly. If $\alpha=[a_0;a_1,a_2,\dots]$ has convergents $\frac{p_n}{q_n}$, then
$$\frac{1}{q_n(q_n+q_{n+1})}<\Bigl|\alpha-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\Bigr|<\frac1{q_nq_{n+1}},\qquad q_{n+1}=a_{n+1}q_n+q_{n-1}.$$
So a large partial quotient $a_{n+1}$ means an unusually good approximation $\frac{p_n}{q_n}$. For $\pi=[3;7,15,1,292,\dots]$ the convergent $\frac{355}{113}$ is followed by $a_4=292$, which explains its accuracy.

Three further facts, all classical:
- Legendre: if $|\alpha-\frac pq|<\frac1{2q^2}$, then $\frac pq$ is a convergent of $\alpha$.
- Hurwitz: every irrational $\alpha$ has infinitely many $\frac pq$ with $|\alpha-\frac pq|<\frac1{\sqrt5\,q^2}$, and $\sqrt5$ cannot be replaced by any larger constant when $\alpha=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2=[1;1,1,\dots]$.
- $\alpha$ is badly approximable, meaning $|\alpha-\frac pq|>\frac c{q^2}$ for some $c>0$ and all $\frac pq$, exactly when its partial quotients are bounded. Quadratic irrationals have eventually periodic expansions and are therefore badly approximable.

So the exponent $2$ in Dirichlet's theorem cannot be improved for any quadratic irrational, and the constant matters only up to a bounded factor.

blocks.title: Liouville's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic number of degree $d\ge2$. There is a constant $c(\alpha)>0$ such that
$$\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|>\frac{c(\alpha)}{q^d}\qquad\text{for all integers }p\text{ and }q\ge1.$$
In particular $\mu(\alpha)\le d$.

Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ with integer coefficients, of degree $d$. It is irreducible of degree at least $2$, so it has no rational roots, and $f(\frac pq)\ne0$. The number $q^df(\frac pq)$ is a nonzero integer, hence $|f(\frac pq)|\ge q^{-d}$.

Let $M=\max\{|f'(x)|:|x-\alpha|\le1\}$, which is positive. If $|\alpha-\frac pq|\le1$, the mean value theorem gives some $\xi$ between them with
$$q^{-d}\le\Bigl|f\Bigl(\frac pq\Bigr)\Bigr|=\Bigl|f(\alpha)-f\Bigl(\frac pq\Bigr)\Bigr|=|f'(\xi)|\,\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|\le M\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|.$$
If $|\alpha-\frac pq|>1$ then trivially $|\alpha-\frac pq|>q^{-d}$. So any $c(\alpha)<\min(1,1/M)$ works.

blocks.title: From Liouville to Roth
blocks.body:
Liouville's bound is easy because it uses only one polynomial. Improving the exponent $d$ needed a much deeper idea: construct an auxiliary polynomial in several variables that vanishes to high order at $(\alpha,\dots,\alpha)$, and show that two or more very good approximations would force it to vanish where it cannot. The history of the exponent for algebraic $\alpha$ of degree $d$:
- Liouville (1844): $d$.
- Thue (1909): $\frac d2+1+\varepsilon$.
- Siegel (1921): about $2\sqrt d$.
- Dyson (1947): about $\sqrt{2d}$.
- Roth (1955): $2+\varepsilon$, independent of $d$, which is best possible by Dirichlet. Roth received the Fields Medal in 1958.

blocks.title: Roth's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic irrational number and $\varepsilon>0$. Then
$$\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|<\frac{1}{q^{2+\varepsilon}}$$
has only finitely many solutions in rationals $\frac pq$ with $q\ge1$. Equivalently, $\mu(\alpha)=2$.

blocks.title: What Roth does not say
blocks.body:
Roth's theorem is ineffective: the proof shows there are finitely many exceptions but gives no way to bound them, so it cannot be used to list the solutions of an equation. Effective results with weaker exponents come from Baker's theory of linear forms in logarithms.

It also does not say whether $\varepsilon$ can be removed. For quadratic irrationals it can (they are badly approximable). For algebraic numbers of degree at least $3$, such as $\sqrt[3]2$, it is unknown whether the partial quotients are bounded; no example is known either way.

The exponent $2$ is not special to algebraic numbers. Khintchine's theorem says that if $\psi$ is positive and non-increasing, then for almost every real $\alpha$ the inequality $|q\alpha-p|<\psi(q)$ has infinitely many solutions if $\sum_q\psi(q)$ diverges, and only finitely many if it converges. With $\psi(q)=q^{-1-\varepsilon}$ the series converges, so almost every $\alpha$ has $\mu(\alpha)=2$. The Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture, a version without monotonicity for reduced fractions, was proved by Koukoulopoulos and Maynard (2020). The exceptional set $\{\alpha:\mu(\alpha)\ge\tau\}$ has Lebesgue measure zero for $\tau>2$ and Hausdorff dimension $2/\tau$ (Jarník, Besicovitch).

blocks.title: Irrationality proofs are approximation statements
blocks.body: Turn the question around. Rationals are very badly approximated by other rationals: if $\alpha=\frac ab$ and $\frac pq\ne\alpha$, then $|\alpha-\frac pq|=\frac{|aq-bp|}{bq}\ge\frac1{bq}$. This gives a criterion for irrationality.

blocks.title: Irrationality criterion
blocks.body:
Let $\alpha$ be real. If there are integers $p_n,q_n$ with $q_n\alpha-p_n\ne0$ for all $n$ and $q_n\alpha-p_n\to0$, then $\alpha$ is irrational.

Quantitative form: if moreover $\frac1n\log|q_n|\to\log Q$ and $\frac1n\log|q_n\alpha-p_n|\to-\log E$ with $Q>1$ and $E>1$, then $\mu(\alpha)\le1+\frac{\log Q}{\log E}$.

blocks.title: Proof of the qualitative criterion
blocks.body: Suppose $\alpha=\frac ab$ with $b\ge1$. Then $b(q_n\alpha-p_n)=aq_n-bp_n$ is a nonzero integer, so $|q_n\alpha-p_n|\ge\frac1b$ for all $n$, contradicting $q_n\alpha-p_n\to0$. (The quantitative form is proved by comparing a hypothetical very good approximation $\frac pq$ with the forms $q_n\alpha-p_n$ for a suitably chosen $n$; we omit it.)

blocks.title: Two irrationality proofs
blocks.body:
The number $e$. Let $q_n=n!$ and $p_n=n!\sum_{k\le n}\frac1{k!}$, an integer. Then
$$0<q_ne-p_n=\sum_{k>n}\frac{n!}{k!}=\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{(n+1)(n+2)}+\cdots<\sum_{j\ge1}\frac1{(n+1)^j}=\frac1n,$$
so $e$ is irrational by the criterion. (Here $q_n$ grows faster than exponentially, so the quantitative form does not apply; in fact $\mu(e)=2$, which follows from its explicit continued fraction $[2;1,2,1,1,4,1,1,6,\dots]$.)

Apéry's theorem (1978): $\zeta(3)$ is irrational. Apéry found integers $a_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}k^2$ and rationals $b_n$ with $2\,d_n^3b_n\in\mathbb Z$, where $d_n=\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,n)$, such that
$$0<|a_n\zeta(3)-b_n|\ \text{decays like}\ (1+\sqrt2)^{-4n},\qquad a_n\ \text{grows like}\ (1+\sqrt2)^{4n},$$
up to polynomial factors; both satisfy $$n^3u_n=(34n^3-51n^2+27n-5)u_{n-1}-(n-1)^3u_{n-2}$$. By the prime number theorem $d_n=e^{n(1+o(1))}$. Put $q_n=2d_n^3a_n$ and $p_n=2d_n^3b_n$. Then $|q_n|$ grows like $Q^n$ with $Q=e^3(1+\sqrt2)^4$ and $|q_n\zeta(3)-p_n|$ decays like $E^{-n}$ with $E=(1+\sqrt2)^4/e^3$. The key numerical fact is $E>1$: $4\log(1+\sqrt2)\approx3.5255>3$. So $\zeta(3)$ is irrational, and the quantitative criterion gives $\mu(\zeta(3))\le1+\frac{3+4\log(1+\sqrt2)}{4\log(1+\sqrt2)-3}\approx13.42$. No analogous construction is known for $\zeta(5)$. Later work showed that infinitely many of the values $\zeta(3),\zeta(5),\zeta(7),\dots$ are irrational (Ball and Rivoal) and that at least one of $\zeta(5),\zeta(7),\zeta(9),\zeta(11)$ is irrational (Zudilin), but no specific odd value beyond $\zeta(3)$ is known to be irrational.

blocks.title: Example 1: approximating √2
blocks.body: The convergents of $\sqrt2=[1;2,2,2,\dots]$ are $1,\frac32,\frac75,\frac{17}{12},\frac{41}{29},\frac{99}{70},\dots$ Show that each satisfies $p^2-2q^2=\pm1$, and deduce that $q^2|\sqrt2-\frac pq|\to\frac1{2\sqrt2}\approx0.354$.
blocks.solution:
The convergents satisfy $p_{n+1}=2p_n+p_{n-1}$, $q_{n+1}=2q_n+q_{n-1}$; equivalently $p_{n+1}+q_{n+1}\sqrt2=(p_n+q_n\sqrt2)(1+\sqrt2)$. Since $(1+\sqrt2)(1-\sqrt2)=-1$, the norm $p^2-2q^2$ changes sign at each step and keeps absolute value $1$: $1-2=-1$, $9-8=1$, $49-50=-1$, $289-288=1$, $1681-1682=-1$, $9801-9800=1$. These are the solutions of [[pell|Pell's equation]] $p^2-2q^2=\pm1$.

Then $|p-q\sqrt2|=\frac{|p^2-2q^2|}{p+q\sqrt2}=\frac1{p+q\sqrt2}$, so
$$q^2\Bigl|\sqrt2-\frac pq\Bigr|=\frac{q}{p+q\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{p/q+\sqrt2}\to\frac1{2\sqrt2}.$$
For $\frac{99}{70}$ the value is $0.35354\ldots$. So $\sqrt2$ is approximated to order exactly $q^{-2}$, never better: it is badly approximable, as every quadratic irrational is.

blocks.title: Example 2: |sin n| is often small
blocks.body: Prove that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ with $|\sin n|<\frac5n$.
blocks.solution:
By Dirichlet's theorem applied to $\pi$ there are infinitely many fractions $\frac nm$ with $m\ge1$ and $|\pi-\frac nm|<\frac1{m^2}$, i.e. $|m\pi-n|<\frac1m$. Since $\sin$ has period $\pi$ up to sign and $|\sin x|\le|x|$,
$$|\sin n|=|\sin(n-m\pi)|\le|n-m\pi|<\frac1m.$$
Also $n<m\pi+\frac1m\le m(\pi+1)<5m$, so $\frac1m<\frac5n$. As the fractions are distinct and $|\frac nm-\pi|\to0$, the denominators $m$ are unbounded and hence so are the $n\approx m\pi$; infinitely many $n$ occur.

For instance $n=355$: $355\,|\sin355|\approx0.0107$, far below $5$.

blocks.title: Example 3: Liouville's number is transcendental
blocks.body: Let $\lambda=\sum_{k\ge1}10^{-k!}=0.110001000\ldots$. Show that $\lambda$ is not algebraic.
blocks.solution:
Let $q_n=10^{n!}$ and $p_n=q_n\sum_{k\le n}10^{-k!}$, an integer. Since $(n+1)!+j\le(n+1+j)!$ for $j\ge0$, the tail satisfies
$$0<\lambda-\frac{p_n}{q_n}=\sum_{k>n}10^{-k!}\le10^{-(n+1)!}\sum_{j\ge0}10^{-j}=\frac{10}{9}\,10^{-(n+1)!}<\frac{2}{q_n^{\,n+1}}.$$
If $\lambda$ were algebraic of degree $d\ge2$, Liouville's theorem would give $\frac{c}{q_n^d}<\frac{2}{q_n^{n+1}}$, i.e. $q_n^{\,n+1-d}<\frac2c$, false for large $n$. If $\lambda$ were rational, $\lambda=\frac ab$, then $\lambda-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\ne0$ would be at least $\frac1{bq_n}$, again contradicting the bound for large $n$. So $\lambda$ is transcendental, with $\mu(\lambda)=\infty$.

blocks.title: Example 4: a Thue equation
blocks.body: Let $m\ne0$ be an integer. Show that $x^3-2y^3=m$ has only finitely many integer solutions.
blocks.solution:
Let $\theta=\sqrt[3]2$ and $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$. Over $\mathbb C$,
$$x^3-2y^3=(x-\theta y)(x-\omega\theta y)(x-\omega^2\theta y).$$
For $y\ne0$ and $j=1,2$, the imaginary part of $x-\omega^j\theta y$ is $\mp\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\theta y$, so $|x-\omega^j\theta y|\ge\frac{\sqrt3}2\theta|y|$. Hence
$$|x-\theta y|\le\frac{|m|}{\frac34\theta^2y^2},\qquad\Bigl|\theta-\frac xy\Bigr|\le\frac{4|m|}{3\theta^2|y|^3}.$$
For $|y|$ large the right side is smaller than $|y|^{-5/2}$. By Roth's theorem with $\varepsilon=\frac12$ (Thue's exponent $\frac32+1+\varepsilon<3$ already suffices) only finitely many fractions $\frac xy$ satisfy this. Each fraction $\frac{x_0}{y_0}$ in lowest terms gives solutions $(kx_0,ky_0)$ only when $k^3\mid m$, so finitely many $k$. Solutions with $y=0$ need $x^3=m$, at most one. Hence finitely many solutions in total.

For $m=1$ a search over $|x|,|y|\le200$ finds only $(1,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. The argument cannot prove the list is complete, because Roth's theorem is ineffective; completing it needs effective methods.

blocks.body:
- Roth's theorem needs $\alpha$ irrational. For rational $\alpha=\frac ab$ the pairs $(ka,kb)$ give $|\alpha-\frac pq|=0$ infinitely often, which is why the definition of $\mu$ requires $0<|\alpha-\frac pq|$.
- Exponent $2$ does not make a number algebraic: almost every real number has $\mu=2$. Only $\mu>2$ rules out algebraicity.
- Most transcendental numbers, including $e$ and $\pi$, are not Liouville numbers; Liouville's method proves transcendence only for very special numbers.
- "Infinitely often" is not "for all $q$": for most $q$ the best approximation is only of order $\frac1q$.
- Roth's theorem is ineffective; it cannot be used to find all solutions of an equation.

[[continued-fractions]] are the computational heart of the subject, and [[pell|Pell's equation]] is the statement that quadratic irrationals have approximations of exact order $q^{-2}$. Approximation theorems give finiteness results for [[diophantine|Diophantine equations]]: Thue equations directly, and integral points on curves, including [[elliptic-curves]], through Siegel's theorem. Dirichlet's theorem is the first step in splitting the circle into major and minor arcs in the [[circle-method]] and in bounding [[exponential-sums]] such as Weyl sums. The distribution of $\{n\alpha\}$ modulo $1$, measured by [[discrepancy]], is controlled by the partial quotients of $\alpha$. Irrationality of values of the [[zeta|zeta function]] is the most famous application of the criterion.

1. Show that $\mu(\alpha)=1$ for every rational $\alpha$.
2. Use Dirichlet's theorem to show that for irrational $\alpha$ the set $\{\{n\alpha\}:n\ge1\}$ is dense in $[0,1)$.
3. Show that if the partial quotients of $\alpha$ are bounded by $K$, then $|\alpha-\frac pq|>\frac{1}{(K+2)q^2}$ for all convergents $\frac pq$.
4. Use Roth's theorem to show that $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-3^k}$ is transcendental.
